summary: Extends LDAP search so a client can ask for all attributes of a given object class to be returned. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Instead of listing each field you want, you say give me everything a person entry has.

questions: ldap request attributes by object class
ldap search return all class attributes
subtitle: Request all attributes of a directory object class in one go.

tldr.problem: LDAP clients can request all user attributes with '*' or all operational attributes with '+', but there is no shorthand to request all attributes that belong to a specific object class, such as a person or a machine.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4529 adds a syntax where a client prefixes an object class name with '@' (for example, '@person') to request all attributes defined for that object class.
tldr.outcome: Clients can write shorter, simpler search requests and URLs. This is especially useful in browser LDAP URLs where users manually type search criteria.

today: RFC 4529 is informational and describes an LDAP extension for requesting attributes by object class. It remains a useful feature for browser-based LDAP searches and provisioning tools.

sections.title: The Shorthand Problem
sections.content:
The Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) lets clients search a directory and specify which attributes to return. Two special shortcuts exist: '*' for all user attributes and '+' for all operational attributes. However, there is no easy way to say 'give me all attributes for a person' or 'give me all attributes for a network machine' without listing every attribute name individually.

This is inconvenient when clients (like web browsers) let users manually type LDAP search URLs or when provisioning tools need to fetch standard attributes for common object types.
sections.plainLanguage: Directory entries come in kinds: a person, a machine, an organization. Each kind has its own set of fields. LDAP has shortcuts for 'all user fields' or 'all system fields', but not for 'all person fields'.

sections.title: The Object Class Selector
sections.content:
RFC 4529 extends LDAP search requests to accept object class identifiers prefixed with the '@' character (called COMMERCIAL AT in the RFC). When a client requests an attribute named '@person', the server treats it as if the client had listed all attributes defined for the person object class, whether they are required by 'MUST' or optional by 'MAY' directives.

The object class can be specified by its short name (like '@person') or by its object identifier number (OID). If the server does not recognize the object class, it treats it as an unknown attribute and behaves accordingly.
sections.plainLanguage: You write '@person' instead of 'name, email, phone, office, ...' and the directory knows to return all the standard person fields. The @ sign tells it you mean an object class, not a single field.

sections.title: Server Support and Extensibility
sections.content:
Servers that support this feature publish an object identifier (OID) 1.3.6.1.4.1.4203.1.5.2 in their 'supportedFeatures' attribute. Clients that support the feature should check for this OID before using the '@' syntax.

The RFC defines an optional 'options' field for future extensibility (for example, to request only required attributes or only optional attributes), though no options are defined in this RFC.
sections.plainLanguage: Servers announce if they support this feature. Clients can ask first: 'Do you handle @person?' and only use it if the server says yes.

sections.title: Primary Use Cases
sections.content:
The RFC identifies the main use case as user-directed LDAP searches, such as when a web browser prompts a user to type an LDAP URL. For example, a user might enter 'ldap:///dc=example,dc=com?@organization?base' to retrieve all attributes of the organization object class without needing to know or type every field name.

This is also useful in administration and provisioning where tools want to fetch a standard set of attributes for common entry types.
sections.plainLanguage: This is mainly for when a person types an LDAP search URL in a web browser or when a tool wants to say 'show me a standard organization entry without me spelling out every field'.

sections.title: Security and Status
sections.content:
RFC 4529 is informational. The RFC notes that this extension does not raise additional security concerns beyond standard LDAP search security, because the attributes that can be requested are exactly the ones that could be listed individually.

The OID 1.3.6.1.4.1.4203.1.5.2 was assigned by the OpenLDAP Foundation under its private enterprise allocation and has been registered with IANA.
sections.plainLanguage: This feature is safe because it just saves you from typing. It does not reveal anything or change access rules. It is an informational RFC that describes a helpful LDAP extension.
